title: The hypertrophy series: utilizing back-off sets to accumulate quality tonnage
summary: NH defines back-off sets as challenging sets in a relevant intensity window after strength work, not light finishers, and describes three approaches: same lift, a close variation, or his own speed back-offs. He explains how each one trades progression on the strength work against the back-off, and calls back-off sets a must for hypertrophy.
claims: Standard back-off sets: after strength work on a compound, do extra sets of the same lift at lower weight; you are already warm so no time is wasted
Back-offs carry slight lack of intensity due to pre-fatigue from the strength work, which is normal
Always doing intensity on strength work and volume on back-offs limits programming; you can invert it, e.g. high-rep strength work then low-rep back-offs
Absolute intensity is dictated by weight: a heavy 8-rep set is higher intensity than a lighter 3-rep set
Taking a plate off after 205 for 6-7 on bench and doing 135 AMRAP is a finisher, not a back-off set; it sits in an irrelevant intensity window
Back-off weight must correlate strictly with strength-work weight and push you to failure within a sensible rep range; find the drop by experimenting
Do 3-4 back-off sets; 10 sets is pointless
Per description, classic back-offs sit around 70-80% intensity, taken to failure, 3-4 sets; highest carryover and tonnage, but high cardio and endurance demand, overuse risk and fatigue
People attacked his speed pulls video title; it was not speed work in the strength sense, speed is just the value dictating progression
Variation back-offs should stay as close in specificity as possible; a front squat after back squats is a new exercise needing a new warm-up, not a back-off
Good close variations: paused squat for squat, paused or deficit deadlift for deadlift, paused bench, close-grip bench or Spoto press for bench
Variations feed the main lift less but can work around overuse injuries and fix weak points, e.g. paused squats if you struggle out of the hole
He always does paused squats and paused bench as back-offs because pushing his squat and bench is not a priority; his chest and quads are already big
If you want strength-work progression, do back-offs in the same style
It is hard to progress on both strength work and back-offs; with same-style back-offs the strength work progresses and back-offs follow by trickle-down
With a variation, you can choose to keep the main lift fixed and push progression on the back-off; less trickle-down, but technically and injury-wise more beneficial
Speed back-offs: after normal strength work do 3-4 sets of the same lift at a weight that goes up without grinding; every rep must be as fast as the last
Speed work at 40% of 1RM is junk volume for hypertrophy; strength blocks are not useful for bodybuilders
Speed back-off weight should be well above 40%, in a small range of 3-4 reps; he does 4 sets of 3 on speed pulls
No weight is added until every rep of every set goes up without a grind; focusing on speed makes failure creep in so sets end in higher intensity than expected
Speed back-offs nearly stall progression on that lift, so use them only with an aggressive strength scheme for the lift or for a lift you do not care to progress
Speed back-offs are fast, accumulate quality tonnage and enforce technique since bad form causes grinding
For deadlifts he prefers speed back-offs over normal back-offs
Apply speed back-offs only to main compounds: bench, squat, deadlift, OHP, possibly weighted pull-ups; not rows, not paused variations
Back-off sets for main movements are a must for hypertrophy: free tonnage with low injury risk
exercises: fixes bottom weakness; his default squat back-off
Paused bench / close-grip bench / Spoto press
4x3, no grind, every rep same speed
